summary: Recommends that DNS resolvers and recursive servers automatically serve certain zones locally unless configured otherwise. It extends the practice from the IPv6 case in RFC 4193 to the in-addr.arpa zones for RFC 1918 private address space and other well-known zones, keeping pointless queries off the public Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: Some DNS lookups ask for the name of an address that only makes sense inside one network, such as an address from the private range 10.0.0.0. This document says that servers should answer those lookups themselves instead of sending them out to the public Internet, where they only cause trouble.

subtitle: Why DNS servers should answer reverse lookups for private address space themselves instead of passing the queries on.

tldr.problem: Reverse lookups for private and special-use address space leak onto the public Internet, load the root servers and force operators to run sacrificial servers that absorb the traffic.
tldr.mechanism: Resolvers and recursive servers should answer queries for a list of reverse zones locally, most easily by serving empty zones that return a name error, with a way to turn the behaviour off zone by zone.
tldr.outcome: Published as Best Current Practice 163 in July 2011, it is the recommendation that keeps private reverse lookups inside the network that owns them.

today: RFC 6303 is Best Current Practice 163, published in July 2011. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and the IANA registry it introduced remains the list of reverse zones that resolvers are expected to serve locally.

sections.title: Why Some DNS Queries Should Stay Local
sections.content:
Experience with the Domain Name System has shown that there are a number of DNS zones that all iterative resolvers and recursive nameservers SHOULD serve automatically, unless they are configured otherwise. RFC 4193 already asks for this to happen for the zone D.F.IP6.ARPA, and this document extends the practice to the IN-ADDR.ARPA zones for RFC 1918 address space and to other well-known zones with similar characteristics.

The reason is measured leakage. Despite instructions to restrict them, queries for these namespaces are still escaping onto the public Internet, and the load has grown large enough that sacrificial nameservers have had to be deployed to protect the parent nameservers for these zones from excessive, unintentional query load. Every expectation is that the load will continue to increase unless steps are taken as described here.

Clients behind badly configured firewalls make the problem worse. A firewall that allows outgoing queries for these namespaces but drops the responses puts a significant load on the root servers, since forward zones are configured but reverse zones are not. It also creates work for the root server operators, who have to reply to enquiries about why the root servers appear to be attacking those clients. Changing the default configuration addresses all of this for the zones on the list.
sections.plainLanguage: Lookups for addresses that only exist inside one network should never travel across the public Internet. This document tells DNS servers to answer those lookups themselves, so the traffic stays where it belongs.

sections.title: Effect on Sites Using Private Addresses
sections.content:
For most sites that use RFC 1918 addresses, the change has little or no detrimental effect. If the site has not already populated its reverse tree, the only effect is that name error responses are generated locally rather than remotely. For sites that do have the reverse tree populated, most either keep a local copy of the zones or forward the queries to servers that have a local copy, so the recommendation does not apply to them.

The most significant impact falls on sites that use delegations for RFC 1918 addresses and have populated those zones. These sites need to override the default configuration described in the document so that resolution continues to work. Typically such sites are fully disconnected from the Internet and run their own root servers for their own non-Internet DNS tree.
sections.plainLanguage: Most networks will not notice the change. A network that runs its own private DNS tree, with its own copies of the private reverse zones, has to switch the new behaviour off for those zones.

sections.title: How a Resolver Should Answer
sections.content:
Unless configured otherwise, an iterative resolver returns authoritatively, with the AA flag set, a name error with RCODE 3 for queries inside the zones listed in Section 4. The exception is a query for the zone name itself, where SOA, NS and "no data" responses are returned as appropriate to the query type. One common way to do all of this at once is to serve empty zones, that is, zones with only an SOA and an NS record.

An implementation of this recommendation MUST provide a mechanism to disable the new behaviour, and SHOULD allow that decision on a zone-by-zone basis. When using empty zones, an implementation SHOULD NOT use the same NS and SOA records as the public Internet servers use, because that would make it harder to detect where the responses came from and therefore harder to detect any leakage to the public Internet servers. It is RECOMMENDED that the NS record default to the name of the zone and that the SOA MNAME default to the name of the only NS record's target. The SOA RNAME SHOULD default to nobody.invalid.. Implementations SHOULD provide a mechanism to set these values, and no address records need to be provided for the nameserver.

The SOA record is needed to support negative caching of the name error responses and to point clients to the primary master for dynamic updates. The SOA values of particular importance are the MNAME, the TTL of the SOA record and the negative TTL, and both TTL values SHOULD match. The remaining SOA timer values MAY be chosen arbitrarily, because they are not intended to control any zone transfer activity. The NS record is needed because some UPDATE clients use NS queries to discover the zone to be updated, and having no address records for the nameserver is expected to abort UPDATE processing in the client.
sections.plainLanguage: The server should say "no such name" itself, and it should say it authoritatively so that other servers cache the answer. It also needs a switch to turn this off for zones a network really does serve.

sections.title: The Zones on the List
sections.content:
The initial list of zones is the content of the IANA registry described in Section 6, and it contains only reverse zones for permanently assigned address space. The zone name is the thing registered.

The RFC 1918 zones cover the IPv4 address space reserved for private internets: 10.IN-ADDR.ARPA, the sixteen zones 16.172.IN-ADDR.ARPA through 31.172.IN-ADDR.ARPA, and 168.192.IN-ADDR.ARPA. The zones from RFC 5735 and RFC 5737 cover ranges that are not expected to appear as source or destination addresses on the public Internet, so there are no globally unique names for them: 0.IN-ADDR.ARPA for the IPv4 "THIS" NETWORK, 127.IN-ADDR.ARPA for the IPv4 loopback network, 254.169.IN-ADDR.ARPA for IPv4 link local, 2.0.192.IN-ADDR.ARPA for TEST-NET-1, 100.51.198.IN-ADDR.ARPA for TEST-NET-2, 113.0.203.IN-ADDR.ARPA for TEST-NET-3 and 255.255.255.255.IN-ADDR.ARPA for IPv4 broadcast.

The IPv6 zones cover the reverse mappings for the IPv6 unspecified and loopback addresses, the zone D.F.IP6.ARPA required by Section 4.4 of RFC 4193, the four IPv6 link-local zones 8.E.F.IP6.ARPA, 9.E.F.IP6.ARPA, A.E.F.IP6.ARPA and B.E.F.IP6.ARPA, and the IPv6 example prefix zone 8.B.D.0.1.0.0.2.IP6.ARPA.

The document adds a caution about the loopback zone: serving an empty 127.IN-ADDR.ARPA is not an attempt to discourage a network from providing a PTR record for 1.0.0.127.IN-ADDR.ARPA locally. A meaningful reverse mapping should exist, but the exact setup is out of scope, and the same logic applies to the reverse mapping for ::1. The recommendations simply assume that no other coverage for these domains exists.
sections.plainLanguage: The list covers the reverse zones for private IPv4 space, several special-use IPv4 ranges, and the IPv6 zones for loopback, link-local and locally assigned addresses.

sections.title: Zones That Are Out of Scope
sections.content:
IPv6 site-local addresses, which are deprecated, and IPv6 non-locally assigned local addresses from RFC 4193 are not covered. IPv6 site-local addresses are expected to correct themselves as implementations drop support for them, although sacrificial servers for the zones C.E.F.IP6.ARPA through F.E.F.IP6.ARPA may still be needed in the short term if the traffic becomes excessive.

For IPv6 non-locally assigned local addresses, where L is 0, no decision has been made about whether the Regional Internet Registries will provide delegations in that space. If they do not, C.F.IP6.ARPA will need to be added to the list. If they do, the registries will need to make sure that nameservers are provided for those addresses.

IP6.INT was once used to provide reverse mapping for IPv6. It was deprecated in RFC 4159 and the delegation was removed from the INT zone in June 2006. Legacy software may still send queries for names under the IP6.INT domain, but this document does not treat IP6.INT as a local zone. The document has also deliberately left alone the names immediately under the root domain. Some of that traffic, such as lookups for .local or .workgroup and for IPv4 addresses, could be handled with these techniques, but there is a far larger amount of traffic that needs a different strategy, such as lookups for unqualified hostnames and for IPv6 addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Some reverse zones are deliberately left out, including the old IPv6 site-local range and the IP6.INT zone that was withdrawn years ago.

sections.title: The Registry of Zones
sections.content:
IANA has established a registry of the zones that require this default behaviour, and the initial contents of that registry are the zones in Section 4. Implementors are encouraged to check the registry periodically and adjust their implementations to follow any change.

The registry can be amended through IETF Review as described in RFC 5226. As part of that review, it should be noted that once a zone is added it is effectively added permanently: once an address range starts being configured as a local zone in systems across the Internet, reversing those changes becomes impossible.

IANA should coordinate with the Regional Internet Registries to ensure that, as DNSSEC is deployed in the reverse tree, delegations for these zones are made in the manner described in Section 7.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of zones lives in an IANA registry, and software is expected to keep up with it. Adding a zone is a one-way step in practice, because once networks start answering for it locally there is no going back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
During the initial deployment phase, particularly where RFC 1918 addresses are in use, some clients may unexpectedly receive a name error rather than a PTR record. That may cause service disruption until their recursive nameservers have been reconfigured.

As DNSSEC is deployed within the IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA namespaces, the zones on the list will need to be delegated as insecure delegations, or be within insecure zones. That allows DNSSEC validation to succeed for queries in these spaces even though the answers do not come from the delegated servers.

It is recommended that sites actively using these namespaces secure them with DNSSEC (RFC 4035) by publishing and using DNSSEC trust anchors. That protects clients from accidentally importing unsigned responses from the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Turning this on can briefly break lookups that used to work, and the reverse tree needs DNSSEC to be handled carefully so that unsigned answers cannot slip in from elsewhere.
